title: Infra CI/CD, IaC Modules, and GPU Fleet Playbook
author: Marcus Lin
body:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook codifies the operational standards and end-to-end processes for Redwood's infrastructure engineering surface that affects GPU fleet capacity, cloud accounts and networking, Terraform/IaC modules, CI/CD build pipelines, and runbooks. It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and on-call responders.

Scope:
- Cloud accounts (AWS primary, GCP for experimental clusters)
- VPC/networking patterns and cross-account networking
- Terraform modules and versioning policies
- CI/CD pipelines for infra modules and GPU image builds
- Fleet capacity planning, autoscaling, and runbooks for common incidents

Ownership and contacts
- Primary owner: infra-engineering team (eng-infra)
- Service/Component owners:
  - gpu-manager (capacity/autoscaling): Diego Morales
  - node-provisioner (spot/ondemand lifecycle): Priya Sharma
  - infra-ci (Terraform lint/plan/apply pipelines): Marcus Lin
- Pager rotation: infra-oncall (primary), infra-sre (secondary)

SLOs and operational targets
- Control plane availability for gpu-manager: 99.95% monthly
- Median GPU allocation latency (cold start): < 45s
- 95th percentile GPU allocation latency (steady-state): < 120s
- Terraform plan apply success rate (main branches): >= 98%
- CI pipeline queue time for infra changes: < 10 minutes

High-level architecture and services
- VPCs and networking: redwood-core-vpc (shared services), redwood-gpu-vpc-<env> (per-account/per-region)
- Fleet manager: gpu-manager (k8s controller + standalone scheduler)
- Node provisioning: node-provisioner (Cloud Provider API + Instance store)
- Capacity autoscaler: capacity-autoscaler (integrates with gpu-manager metrics and cluster autoscaler)
- IaC modules: terraform-aws-network, terraform-aws-gpu-instance, terraform-aws-eks, terraform-aws-iam-kit
- CI/CD: infra-ci (GitHub Actions) and infra-deploy (ArgoCD for cluster-level manifests)

Cloud accounts and networking standards
1) Account layout:
   - prod-core (control plane and shared services)
   - prod-gpu-<region>-1 (GPU worker account primary)
   - staging, dev, experimental accounts mirror prod but with reduced quotas
2) VPC design:
   - Default CIDR ranges: 10.<region>.0.0/16 assigned per account to avoid overlap
   - Subnets: public (for NAT gateways/load balancers), private (for GPU nodes), management (for bastion/jump hosts)
   - VPC peering and Transit Gateway: use redwood-network-transit TGW for cross-account routing; no direct VPC peering for prod accounts unless approved
3) Security groups and NACLs:
   - GPU nodes accept traffic from redwood-controlplane SG and trusted monitoring CIDRs only
   - SSH access restricted via SSM Session Manager; no direct SSH allowed by default
4) IP and DNS:
   - Internal DNS zone: redwood.internal. Use Route53 private hosted zones per account and attach to TGW

Terraform / IaC module guidelines
- Repo layout: mono-repo for modules (terraform-modules/) and environment configurations (terraform-environments/).
- Module naming: terraform-aws-<purpose>-v1 (major version included in module name as part of deprecation strategy)
- Versioning and releases: Use semantic version tags (vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH). Modules published to internal registry with changelog.
- Testing: Every module must include unit tests via terratest, a minimal example in examples/, and a smoke deploy pipeline in CI that runs plan/apply/destroy against a non-prod account with restricted resources.
- State: Remote state via S3 (bucket: redwood-tfstate-<env>) with state locking via DynamoDB table redwood-tf-locks. State encryption with default KMS key per account.
- Secrets: Use Vault for dynamic secrets and avoid storing credentials in terraform variables or state. For KMS/SSH keys use encrypted secrets manager or AWS KMS with strict RBAC.

Key modules (examples)
- terraform-aws-network: constructs VPC, subnets, TGW attachments, private zones
- terraform-aws-gpu-instance: launches GPU EC2s (p4d,p4de,p5) with user_data hooks for containerd, NVIDIA drivers and node labels
- terraform-aws-eks: EKS cluster bootstrap with node group integration hooks for gpu instances
- terraform-aws-iam-kit: small reusable IAM constructs for service roles and cross-account assume-role patterns

CI/CD and build pipelines
- infra-ci (GitHub Actions) responsibilities:
  - Lint: tflint, terraform fmt check
  - Unit tests: go/pytest/terratest runs for modules
  - Plan: terraform plan in a sandboxed workspace on PRs with comment output (plan summary + diffstat)
  - Apply: gated to main branch; requires 2 approvers for prod-level envs and preview-approve labels for staging
- GPU image build pipeline: gpu-image-build (Packer + ECR): builds golden AMIs/container images used by node-provisioner, signs artifacts, publishes immutable tags (e.g., gpu-node:v2026.01.05-<hash>)
- Promotion flow: artifacts built in dev account, promoted to staging, then to prod via infra-deploy pipeline with manifests stored in gitops repo
- Secrets in CI: stored in GitHub Actions secrets and retrieved using short-lived tokens; long-lived credentials are avoided.

Change and deployment process (for infra)
1) Create a feature branch in terraform-environments or modules repo.
2) Open PR with description, risk assessment, roll-forward and rollback plan, and a small cost estimate if relevant.
3) CI runs lint/tests/plan. For module changes tests must pass and example deploys must succeed.
4) Approvals: 2 approvers required for infra modules; cross-team reviewers required for networking or security changes.
5) Apply to non-prod via infra-ci apply. Validate metrics for 24 hours.
6) Schedule prod apply in the maintenance window if change affects networking, state, or cross-account roles. Notify oncall and platform teams 48h in advance.

GPU fleet and capacity planning
- Capacity metrics tracked: GPU utilization (per-GPU and per-instance), pending allocation queue length, average allocation latency, spot interruption rate, preemptible reclaim rate.
- Minimum capacity policy: Prod must maintain 20% buffer for critical queues or a hardened burst pool of reserved p4 instances (reserved-pool-<region>).
- Spot vs on-demand strategy: 60% spot for non-latency sensitive jobs; core inference pools require >= 80% on-demand / reserved depending on SLA tier.
- Autoscaling knobs: targetUtilization=0.65, scaleDownDelay=10m, scaleUpCooldown=3m. These are tunable per workload in gpu-manager routing config.
- Forecasting: weekly consumption forecast using Prometheus + historical billing; capacity requests to cloud procurement 2 weeks in advance for on-demand/reserved reservations.

Runbooks and common incident playbooks
- Runbook: GPU allocation failure (high-level)
  1) Detect: Alert when pending allocation queue > 10 for > 5m or median allocation latency > 120s.
  2) Investigate: Check gpu-manager logs, Cloud provider quota, instance launch errors, and capacity-autoscaler scaling events.
  3) Mitigate: If quota, request quota increase via cloud console and start warm instances from reserved pool. If spot preemptions high, move critical workloads to reserved on-demand pool. If API rate-limited, escalate to cloud-accounts-oncall.
  4) Postmortem: Create incident in incident tracker with timeline, root cause, and corrective actions (e.g., change scale thresholds, add fallback model variant routing).

- Runbook: Terraform state corruption / plan drift
  1) Detect: Failed apply with state conflict or drift detected by drift detection job.
  2) Investigate: Check S3 state file, locking table entries, and last successful apply logs.
  3) Mitigate: Restore state from last known good snapshot, unblock lock by clearing DynamoDB lock after confirming no running applies.
  4) Postmortem: Re-run module tests, add additional pre-apply checks to CI.

Operational playbook examples (commands)
- Inspect terraform plan output for PRs:
  - gh pr checkout <pr-number> && terraform init && terraform plan -var-file=env.tfvars
- Force-unlock state (use with caution):
  - aws dynamodb delete-item --table-name redwood-tf-locks --key '{"LockID":{"S":"terraform.tfstate"}}'
- Build GPU image (local dev):
  - packer build -var-file=dev.pkrvars.hcl gpu-node.pkr.hcl

Observability and dashboards
- Key dashboards: GPU Fleet Overview (utilization, allocation latency, pending queue), Cluster Health (node status, driver health), Terraform CI (plan pass rate, queue time), CI artifacts and promotion status.
- Alerts: concise actionable alerts following alerting handbook: stateful runbook reference, owner, severity. Example alert: GPUAllocationLatencyHigh (trigger: median allocation latency > 120s for 5m) -> page infra-oncall, severity P1.

Runbook cadence and maintenance
- Quarterly review: module owners must review and update module examples, tests and upgrade notes each quarter.
- Runbook drills: Semi-annual game days that exercise GPU allocation, state restore, and network partition scenarios.
- Documentation: Keep runbooks in this playbook and link to live-runbook pages in runbooks/. Any change to runbooks must include a short validation checklist executed after the change.

Appendix: useful links and references
- Terraform modules registry: internal://terraform-modules/
- CI pipelines: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra-ci/actions
- GPU runbook (detailed): /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-capacity-and-infra-runbook-2026.json
- Contact: infra-oncall@redwood.company
